answer_en: No official text says in words that an accumulating foreign fund is taxed only when sold, but every current Tax Authority text on foreign funds taxes the holder only on a sale of the unit and on distributions: its 2019 letter to TASE and the banks treats a TASE-registered foreign fund as a unit, sets withholding only on sale and on distributions, and credits only foreign tax on the fund's distributions (accumulating Irish ETFs such as CSPX are among the funds listed on TASE), and the Ordinance has no attribution rule for a non-controlling holder. One older Tax Authority statement points the other way: circular 7/2003 s.4.4 (May 2003, before Amendment 147 rewrote the definition of a security) said that from 2007 a holder of a foreign-resident fund would be taxed 'according to the fund's investments', each time the fund sells assets; no later text applies that.

proposed_rule_text: TXF-11, Rule (replace the reading-only wording): An individual who is not a controlling holder of a listed foreign fund is taxed on two events only: a sale or redemption of the unit (capital gain, TXF-01 to TXF-03) and a distribution (dividend, TXF-08). Income the fund reinvests enters the tax base only through the sale price. For a foreign fund registered on TASE the Tax Authority's letter of 4.7.2019 says a "קרן חוץ" is a unit and sets withholding on sale and on distributions only, with foreign-tax credit only for tax on the fund's own distributions (TXF-05, TXF-06); accumulating Irish UCITS ETFs are among the funds listed on TASE (CSPX factsheet). Conditions / exceptions: no Tax Authority sentence states the rule for accumulating funds in words; it follows from the 2019 letter, the s.88 definition of a security (Amendment 147, 2005: a unit and a security issued abroad are securities) and the absence of any attribution rule for non-controlling holders (s.75B needs control). Contrary: circular 7/2003 s.4.4 (May 2003) said that from 1.1.2007 a holder of a foreign-resident fund would be taxed "לפי השקעות הקרן"; it predates Amendment 147 and no later Tax Authority text applies it. Strength: primary by implication (Tax Authority letter), with one contrary older circular.
site_effect: The accumulating-fund tax dimension can rest on a Tax Authority text (the 2019 letter, by implication) instead of the personal-finance blog, but should keep a caution note naming circular 7/2003 s.4.4; method G-18 numbers do not change (tax at sale only). Still a founder call under D10 whether 'by implication' is enough to drop the caution flag on index-sp500 and brokerage-account.
still_unknown: A Tax Authority sentence on accumulating foreign funds, especially funds bought at a foreign broker rather than registered on TASE; whether circular 7/2003 s.4.4 was ever withdrawn (no notice found); whether funds organised as trusts or contractual funds (FCP) rather than companies would be treated differently.

answer_en: The law lets the year's management and custody fees reduce the gain (reg. 6(a)), lets the bank deduct them at withholding only if the Director approved and under his rules (reg. 8), and turns fees not deducted in the year into a capital loss from securities (s.92(a)(5)); the Tax Authority's 2025 return form counts only transaction commissions in cost and proceeds. No Director's approval or rule under reg. 8, and no Tax Authority or bank text showing banks do it, was found.

proposed_rule_text: TXS-06, Conditions (add): Fees for the year that were not deducted from that year's proceeds count as a capital loss from securities (s.92(a)(5)), so they can offset capital gains and, in the same year, interest or dividends on securities (s.92(a)(4)), and carry forward if a return is filed. Whether a bank or TASE member deducts them at withholding depends on the Director's approval and rules under reg. 8 of the 2002 withholding regulations, which were not found. The 2025 return form 1325 puts only transaction commissions into cost and proceeds ("לא כולל עמלות תקופתיות").
site_effect: Keep method G-20 flagged: the fee deduction is certain only through an annual return (or as a securities loss), not at the bank. Materiality is small: a 0.1% custody fee is worth 0.025% of the balance a year in tax.

answer_en: In practice yes: the Tax Authority says that whoever sold securities without full Israeli withholding 'must file an annual return' and must report and pay an advance by 31 July and 31 January; its 2025 return forms send sales made abroad not through Israeli withholders to forms 1325 and 1322 (appendices to the annual return), and its 2026 refund guide excludes 'trading securities on an external platform' from the short form 135. The regulations leave one narrow exemption (foreign income up to the 375,000 NIS ceiling on which the annual foreign-income advance was paid with its report by 30 April, with no loss offset), but no Tax Authority text says a foreign-broker saver may use it instead of the half-yearly regime; and a loss carries forward only if a return was filed for the loss year.

answer_en: It is simply untaxed and gives no deductible loss: when the inflationary amount is larger than the nominal gain, the whole nominal gain is an exempt inflationary amount and the real gain is zero, and an allowable capital loss is measured in nominal terms only.

site_effect: Confirms F-40's max(0, real gain) with no loss carried; method G-07 can close for this case and its open-question tag can go.

answer_en: The taxable base never exceeds the nominal gain: when the index (the CPI for a shekel fund unit) falls over the holding period, the inflationary amount is zero, not negative, and the whole nominal gain is the real gain. If the sale ends in a nominal loss while the index fell, only the loss left after removing the fall in the index can be offset.

proposed_rule_text: TXS-02, Rule (add): When the index is lower on the sale day than on the purchase day, the inflationary amount is zero, not negative, and the real gain equals the nominal gain; tax can never exceed the rate times the nominal gain. If the sale ends in a nominal loss, the part of the loss equal to the fall in the index (a "negative inflationary amount") is not allowed and only the rest can be offset. Source: circular 10/2025 appendix (examples 3 and 4), applying ע"א 3555/15 מוזס (Supreme Court, 12.9.2016). The circular's worked examples use an exchange-rate index; its stated rule covers 'שינוי ערך מדד או … שער חליפין'.
site_effect: F-40 takes the inflationary amount as max(0, …) for gains, so a money-market fund's real gain never exceeds its nominal gain in a deflation; where the engine models losses, the offsettable loss in a deflation is the nominal loss minus the fall in the index. The government-bond-cpi open-question tag and method G-07 can close.
still_unknown: Nothing material. The Supreme Court judgment was read from the capitax copy; the court's own site resets scripted connections (listed as blocked).

answer_en: The Tax Authority's approach is that an Israeli withholder computes the 25% on the gross foreign dividend and may credit the foreign tax actually paid, capped at the treaty rate (or the foreign domestic rate if lower), so it withholds only the difference: with US withholding at the 25% treaty rate (W-8BEN) the Israeli top-up is nil, and an Irish fund's distribution, on which Ireland deducts nothing, bears the full 25% in Israel. This is stated in a published Tax Authority ruling (a US REIT listed on TASE) and in a bank's tax page citing Tax Authority instructions; no general directive to banks was found.

proposed_rule_text: TXF-10, Conditions (replace the open part): The regulation sets 25% on the gross dividend and does not mention foreign tax. In practice the Israeli withholder credits the foreign tax withheld, up to the lower of the tax actually paid and the treaty (or foreign domestic) rate, and withholds only the difference: Tax Authority ruling 5916/20 (a US REIT listed on TASE) says the TASE member withholds on the gross amount "לפני זיכוי בגין מסי חוץ" and "יהא רשאי לתת זיכוי" for US tax actually paid up to the treaty rate; the 2019 'קרן חוץ' letter caps creditable foreign tax the same way; a bank's tax page (Mercantile, Discount group) says the top-up follows this cap "בהתאם להוראות רשות המסים". Result: US dividends with W-8BEN (US 25%, TXF-12) bear no further Israeli withholding; foreign tax above the cap is not credited by the bank. Strength: Tax Authority ruling (case-specific) plus institution practice; no general directive found.
site_effect: For dividends received through an Israeli bank: US stocks or US-domiciled funds total 25% (US 25%, Israeli top-up 0), not 50%; Irish distributing funds 25% in Israel (no Irish tax, TXF-28) on top of the fund-level US 15% that stays a cost (TXF-16). The guide pages that list TXF OQ3 can show this with a 'per Tax Authority ruling and bank practice' caution.
still_unknown: The general Tax Authority instruction to withholders; whether every bank and TASE member applies the credit (the ruling says 'may').

answer_en: Under the US-Ireland treaty an Irish collective investment undertaking is itself an Irish resident, and US dividends paid to it may be taxed by the US at no more than 15%, if it passes the treaty's limitation-on-benefits test (for example, its principal class of shares or units regularly traded on a recognised exchange such as London, Amsterdam or the Irish Stock Exchange). Whether a given fund qualifies and what it actually suffered is a fund fact for its annual report, which was not reached.

proposed_rule_text: TXF-16, Conditions (replace the Q7 sentence): The US-Ireland treaty treats an Irish collective investment undertaking as an Irish resident (Art. 4(1)(d)) and caps US tax on dividends paid to it at 15% (Art. 10(2)(b)), subject to the limitation-on-benefits article (Art. 23: for example units or shares regularly traded on a recognised exchange, which includes London, Amsterdam and the Irish Stock Exchange). The rate a given Irish fund actually bears is that fund's fact (annual report), not a general rule.
site_effect: F-20's fund-level US withholding of 15% for an Irish fund can cite the treaty as the cap, labelled 'treaty rate; the fund's own report not read', instead of an unsourced figure. Compared with holding US shares or US funds directly (US 25%, credited in Israel), the Irish fund's 15% is a non-creditable cost inside the fund (TXF-16).
still_unknown: What a given fund (for example CSPX) reports as US withholding suffered; the iShares literature pages for prospectus and annual report returned a site page instead of the PDF and were not pursued.

answer_en: When the foreign currency weakened against the shekel, the inflationary amount is zero, not negative: tax falls on the whole shekel nominal gain and never more. If the sale ends in a shekel loss, the part of the loss caused by the currency's fall cannot be offset; only the rest is allowable.

proposed_rule_text: TXF-03, Conditions (replace the Q5 sentence): If the currency fell over the holding period, the inflationary amount is zero, not negative: the real gain is the whole shekel nominal gain. If the sale ends in a shekel loss, the part of the loss equal to the currency's fall (original cost × (rate on purchase − rate on sale) / rate on purchase) is not allowable; only the rest can be offset (ע"א 3555/15 מוזס, Supreme Court 12.9.2016; circular 10/2025 appendix, examples 3 and 4). A family company uses the CPI, not the exchange rate (ע"א 1038/17 אור שרה, circular note 13).
site_effect: The engine can compute foreign-currency holdings when the shekel strengthens: inflationary amount = max(0, cost × (rate_sale / rate_buy − 1)); for a loss, allowable loss = nominal loss minus the currency part, floored at 0. Method G-24 can drop TXF OQ5 from the tier-2 blockers (TX2 OQ1 for deposits is a separate question).
still_unknown: Nothing for listed securities held by an individual. The Supreme Court judgment was read from the capitax copy; the court site resets scripted connections.
